messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 38
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Welder
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 60

She is 38, a single woman from a South Eastern Asian family, and she makes her living as a welder. Before the accident, she likes the certainty of metalwork—the way a clean seam answers steady hands, the way heat and pressure can be controlled if she pays attention. She is known at the fabrication shop for being careful, not talkative but dependable. She takes extra shifts, sends money to her mother, and keeps mostly to herself. She says she has always preferred work that lets her focus on something concrete.

The day of the accident begins like any other: loud fans, sparks, the smell of steel and oil. They are behind on an order, and everyone is moving quickly. She is working alongside a younger coworker, a man she has trained on and off for several months. They have done the same sequence many times—cut, tack, reposition, weld. At one point she signals for him to help move a heavy piece into place. Later, when she tells the story, this is where time starts to behave strangely. She remembers noticing one clamp not fully tightened. She remembers thinking, just for a second, that she should stop and reset it. She also remembers the pressure of the day, the impatience in the room, her own decision to go ahead because they are “almost there.”

Then the metal shifts.

She still hears the sound it makes before she sees what has happened: a sudden shriek of steel, then shouting. The beam slips and crushes her coworker’s leg against the table. She remembers dropping her torch, running toward him, seeing his face go gray and stunned before he starts screaming. There is blood on the floor and on her gloves. Someone calls emergency services. Someone else is yelling for a tourniquet. She is kneeling beside him but feels useless, as if her hands no longer belong to her. Later she learns that he survives but with devastating injuries, multiple surgeries, and permanent damage.

In the first days after, she tells everyone the same flat sentence: “It was my fault.” Her supervisor says they are investigating, that there were safety failures and production pressures, that this is not on one person. She hears the words and rejects them immediately. In her mind there is only the image of the loose clamp and the instant when she chooses not to stop. She replays that moment compulsively, as if reviewing it hard enough might reverse it. At night she jerks awake hearing metal scream and his voice calling out. Sometimes she smells hot steel in her apartment and has to turn on all the lights to remind herself where she is.

When she returns to work, the shop feels transformed. The same sparks that once settled her now make her flinch. If someone drops a tool behind her, her whole body snaps tight before she can think. She starts avoiding the bay where it happened, then avoiding any task that involves rigging or repositioning heavy material. She checks clamps over and over, long after others are satisfied, and still does not trust her own eyes. Coworkers begin finishing tasks for her because she freezes at small decisions. She notices their looks and reads judgment in every silence.

Outside work, her life narrows. She stops answering friends from the shop when they invite her for coffee after a shift. She avoids family calls because she cannot bear their concern, and because in her community she feels the weight of shame keenly; she imagines that if they knew the full story, they would hear not an accident but a moral failure. She eats little, loses weight, and spends evenings sitting on the edge of her bed scrolling through old messages from her injured coworker from before the accident, as if those ordinary exchanges belong to another person’s life.

She tells herself she should visit him, but every time she considers it, she is flooded with panic. She imagines seeing his wheelchair, his altered body, his family’s faces. Once she drives to the rehabilitation hospital parking lot and sits gripping the steering wheel until her palms ache, then leaves without going inside. On the way home she hates herself for the relief she feels.

Months pass, and her world remains organized around the accident. She sleeps lightly, waking from dreams in which the beam falls again and again, sometimes onto him, sometimes onto her. She startles easily and scans exits in restaurants, though she rarely stays long enough to eat. She becomes irritable at work, then ashamed of being irritable. There are stretches when she feels almost absent from her own life, moving through shifts and errands as if behind thick glass. The worst moments come unexpectedly: the hiss of a torch, the scrape of a chain, a young man laughing with the same voice as her coworker. Her chest tightens, her thoughts race, and the old sentence returns with punishing certainty—You did this.

Now, when she speaks about herself, she often does so through the language of responsibility and debt. She says she used to trust her hands. She is no longer sure she should be allowed to. Even on quieter days, when she can finish a weld and briefly lose herself in the line of it, the relief is fragile. The accident remains close, waiting inside ordinary sounds and decisions, turning the work she once relied on into a place of fear, vigilance, and grief.
